description: Controlled fire became a technology when people learned to hold hearths at chosen temperatures. At Pinnacle Point, South Africa, silcrete was deliberately heated by about 164,000 years ago, making the stone easier to flake into fine points. Managed fire also cooked food in earth ovens and burned landscapes to renew plants. When hominins first used fire remains debated.

claims: silcrete heated about 164,000 years ago at Pinnacle Point
heating made silcrete easier to flake (pressure flaking)

uncertainty: The earliest use of fire by hominins is debated (claims range over more than a million years); heat treatment at Pinnacle Point (~164 kya) is one well-dated marker of controlled pyrotechnology, and routine use is often placed around 70 kya.

description: A lamp makes fire portable and steady: a hollowed stone holds animal fat that burns on a wick of plant fibre. Lamps gave a small, steady light for working in deep caves.
uncertainty: Wick materials are inferred from residues and experiments; dates for Lascaux are given as roughly 17,000-19,000 years ago depending on the method.

description: Charcoal is wood heated with little air, so water and volatile substances are driven off and nearly pure carbon remains. Burned in earth-covered piles, it gives hotter, cleaner fires than wood, and early metal smelting relied on it. Demand for it consumed woodlands; as charcoal grew costly in Britain, Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke at Coalbrookdale in 1709.

uncertainty: When charcoal was first made deliberately is uncertain; the node dates it with the first smelting (about the sixth to fifth millennium BCE), which varies by region.

description: Bellows force air into a fire, raising its temperature beyond what natural draught allows. Leather bags or skins stretched over clay pots were pumped by hand or foot to feed furnaces. Egyptian tomb paintings of about 1500 BCE show workers treading such bellows; earlier Near Eastern pot-bellows and possible Chalcolithic examples are debated. Medieval blast furnaces later used water-driven bellows.

uncertainty: The earliest bellows are not securely dated: the node uses Egyptian New Kingdom depictions (~1500 BCE), but Near Eastern pot-bellows and possible Chalcolithic finds at Abu Matar may be much earlier.

description: A post mill carries its whole body, sails and gearing on one upright post, so the miller can turn it to face the wind. description: Thomas Newcomen's engine of 1712 used the pressure of the air, not of steam, to do work. Steam filled a cylinder, a jet of cold water condensed it, and the partial vacuum let the atmosphere push a piston down, rocking a beam that worked mine pumps. description: James Watt saw that the atmospheric engine wasted fuel by cooling and reheating its cylinder at every stroke. Engines built by Boulton and Watt from the 1770s used much less coal for the same work, so steam power paid far from coalfields.
uncertainty: Fuel savings varied by engine; figures quoted range widely.

description: Early steam engines pumped water with an up-and-down beam. uncertainty: The sun-and-planet gear is often credited to William Murdoch; it was used partly because James Pickard held a 1780 patent on a crank arrangement.

description: A dynamo turns mechanical work into electric current by spinning coils through a magnetic field, using the induction Michael Faraday discovered in 1831. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated one in 1958, and Robert Noyce at Fairchild devised a planar silicon version in 1959, independently. Patterning by photolithography, related to photographic printing, let factories make many identical chips together.
uncertainty: Kilby and Noyce are both credited; the companies litigated and then cross-licensed. Fairchild's first working monolithic ICs date from May 1960.

description: A microprocessor places a computer's entire central processing unit on one chip. description: A hydroelectric station drops water from a dam or diverted river through turbines that drive generators. The Adams station at Niagara Falls, opened in 1895, was a landmark: from 1896 it sent three-phase alternating current to Buffalo. Large dams later gave cheap continuous power to energy-hungry industries such as aluminium smelting, whose electrolytic process dates from 1886.

claims: Adams plant 1895; Buffalo 1896 by three-phase AC

uncertainty: Small hydroelectric installations predate Niagara (for example Cragside, England, 1878, and Appleton, Wisconsin, 1882); the node dates the dam-scale station from 1895.

description: A photovoltaic cell turns sunlight directly into electric current at a junction between two kinds of semiconductor. Russell Ohl observed the effect in a silicon p-n junction in 1940. In 1954 Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson at Bell Laboratories made a practical silicon cell of about six per cent efficiency; satellites were early users from 1958.
uncertainty: The photovoltaic effect was first observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839 in an electrolytic cell; selenium cells of the 1880s were very inefficient.

description: A lithium-ion battery stores energy by moving lithium ions between two host materials that take them into their crystal layers. John Goodenough's group proposed a lithium cobalt oxide cathode in 1980, Akira Yoshino built a safer cell with a carbon anode in 1985, and commercial sales began in 1991. These light, rechargeable cells suited portable electronics and later electric vehicles.
uncertainty: Stanley Whittingham's 1970s work on intercalation electrodes preceded Goodenough's; the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised all three.

description: A power-station gas turbine burns gas or oil to spin a turbine coupled to a generator, adapting jet-engine principles to continuous duty. In the combined cycle, widely adopted from the 1970s, hot exhaust also raises steam for a second turbine, recovering otherwise wasted heat. Its blades run hotter than ordinary steels tolerate, relying on nickel superalloys such as Nimonic 80.

claims: Nimonic 80 introduced in 1941 and became the standard rotor-blade material of British gas turbines

uncertainty: The first utility gas turbine (Neuchâtel, Switzerland, 1939) predates the node's 1950s date; combined-cycle adoption dates vary by country.

description: Public-key cryptography uses a pair of keys: one can be published so anyone can encrypt messages or check signatures, while only its owner holds the other.
